brief.head: Accidents of history
brief.text: The world does not settle into one equilibrium wherever it starts, Ajay Shah said. Little accidents deep in the past shape how societies, and each of us, unfold. {003-C03}

brief.head: Mirror, mirror
brief.text: We shape ourselves on how we look in other people’s eyes, Amit Varma said. Around Ajay Shah, he would cut out the dad jokes for serious econ talk. {003-J05}

brief.head: How to stay hungry
brief.text: In a winner-takes-all world, Ajay Shah said, long journeys demand rare concentration, or dhyan. Prosaic goals such as making a lot of money peter out too soon. {003-C11}

brief.head: Peers over parents
brief.text: Amit Varma called Judith Rich Harris’s *The Nurture Assumption* one of the seminal social science books of the last century: peers, not parents, shape how children turn out. {003-R09}

brief.head: Law for everyone
brief.text: India’s legal system has some 50 elements needing careful thought, Ajay Shah said, so all of us must engage. “Law is too important to be left to the lawyers.” {003-J08}

thought.text: We should not exaggerate our agency.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, gently doubting that we can choose all the people who shape us

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on masks, accusers and soil
lead.head: The mask that becomes the face
body: Ajay Shah arrived clean-shaven. He had read Vladimir Putin’s claim that everyone supported the invasion of Ukraine except “some bearded intellectuals”, and it inspired him to do something about the beard.
Then he objected. Marx, Engels, Lenin and Trotsky were all bearded, he said: Putin’s own pantheon “should be full of bearded intellectuals”. {003-J01}
It was a light start to an episode about getting stuck.

Amit Varma began in Jaipur, which he visited in January. Its famous pinkness, he learnt, dates only from 1876, when the city was painted to commemorate a visit by Prince Edward. Tourists now come expecting pink, so the fashion in the tourist quarters is to paint everything pink.

People get frozen the same way, Varma argued. A 14-year-old girl praised at family gatherings for her smile and her docility learns that pleasantness wins approval. Boys are pushed to be macho. The persona brings validation, and then it becomes you.
“The mask becomes a person, the persona becomes who you really are,” Varma said. “And that is incredibly dangerous, I think, for people.” {003-C01}
Audiences tighten the mask. Shah’s example was Fox News, whose viewers ran away when it told the truth that Trump had lost. The leader, he said, has to stay with the followers.
## A century to reinvent

What has changed, Shah argued, is time. In the olden days, mean life expectancy at age 20 was about 65, and health declined dramatically from about 50. You became a company man, or spent 35 years as a civil servant wearing one costume.
Today’s 20-year-old, he said, has a hundred years to go, time enough to reinvent oneself many times. “It’s the greatest headroom of all, it’s the greatest luxury,” he said. {003-C05}
Varma once balked at the idea of living to 120: he had watched his father decay and lose his memory. Now he thinks it may make sense to live as if he had 50 years left, even if he has only 20.
## The power to accuse

In the second chapter, Shah turned to fair play in investigation and prosecution. India focuses on political interference, he said, but there is a deeper problem: investigators fall for a pet theory, and confirmation bias does the rest.

His remedy comes in layers. A separate public prosecutor, judged on win rate, should refuse weak cases. A grand jury of citizens adds another check, though in the UK such juries were too often overawed by prosecutors.
In India, he said, the picture is patchy. The income tax department and SEBI run on complete executive discretion; the public prosecutor has withered; the CBI keeps investigator and prosecutor apart.
Varma asked why any government would give up such tools. “The process is a punishment,” he said. {003-C08}
Shah answered with a confession. Laws he had helped amend, when the opportunity was sky high, were not done well, because economists like him lacked knowledge of law and public administration.
## Free books, poor leaves
For his recommendation, Varma urged listeners to read Eamonn Butler’s primers on classical liberalism, Hayek, Mises, Milton Friedman, Adam Smith and public choice, free on the website.
Shah offered an anti-recommendation. Hydroponic leaves look pristine, he said, but without the root microbiome of healthy soil their nutrition is systematically inferior. {003-C12}
The hosts ended at the dinner table: Tolstoy’s live chicken, the promise of lab-grown meat, and fruit flies that lived shorter lives after merely seeing dead ones.

second.label: Captured by the audience
second.head: Fox follows its flock
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why a channel carried the stolen-election theories
body: After the US presidential election, Fox News tried to tell the truth: Trump had lost. Its audience began to run away, Ajay Shah said, and that threatened to become a big financial problem. {003-S03}

So the channel carried the conspiracy theories about a stolen election, to hang on to its viewership. Shah’s lesson: the leader has to stay with the followers, because if the followers are not there, she is not a leader any more.

Amit Varma had made the same point about websites known for one point of view, pro-government or anti-government, which must stay true to that character because it brings traffic. Online, he said, validation makes people double down until “you become that person”. {003-C02}

quote.text: So it was literally a business decision at Fox News to carry the entire conspiracy theories around the stolen election.

second.caption: Fox News and its fleeing viewers

third.head: Flies that saw too much
body: Ajay Shah closed the episode with one last story. In recent scientific experiments, fruit flies were exposed to nothing more than the sight of dead fruit flies. It had an adverse impact on their lifespan. {003-S10}

Amit Varma checked that he had it right: flies that saw dead flies lived shorter lives than those that did not. Shah said humans obviously suffer a moral injury from seeing death, as on a battlefield, and that it extends to other mammals, to birds and all the way down to the fruit fly.
“The mind goes all the way down to flies,” he said.
For Shah, that is reason to respect all life, and to welcome artificial meat. Both hosts are excited by meat grown in a lab, without any animal ever existing. {003-J12}
third.caption: fruit flies that saw dead fruit flies

p2.title: Masks and checks
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on frozen personas, the power to accuse, free primers and living soil

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: Painted pink, stuck pink
sections.caption: the pinkness of Jaipur
body: Amit Varma went to Jaipur in January as a tourist and, because he loves cities, read up on it. The Pink City’s colour, he found, is not old. It was painted pink to commemorate a visit by Prince Edward.

Varma does not know why pink. But the label became a brand the city had to wear. Tourists arrive expecting pink, so the fashion is to paint everything pink. Even people who rebel against the pinkness, he said, end up reinforcing the idea that this is the pink city. {003-S01}
## Social programming

Ajay Shah agreed that we are all creatures of social programming, praised almost at random down certain routes. He likened awareness of it to an AI that understands its operating system: humans, he said, can put their culture under the microscope and wonder whether they could be different. {003-C04}

Varma raised the looking-glass self: we shape ourselves on our reflection in other people’s eyes, so the company we keep matters. Shah was wary of so much calculation. Life throws us in with people, he said, and we are blessed if they are good. {003-C06}
~ Varma quoted John Lennon: life is what happens to you when you’re busy making other plans. Back came the reply: “Or life is what happens to you while you’re busy making podcasts.” {003-J06}

quote.text: Jaipur could have been many things, but it became a pink city.

sections.label: The second idea
sections.head: A jury before the trial
sections.caption: checks on the power to accuse
body: Political interference is not the only thing wrong with investigation and prosecution in India, Ajay Shah said. Investigators are frail and human: they form a pet theory and, through confirmation bias, start seeing only the facts that support it. {003-C07}

His first layer of defence is a separate public prosecutor, a neutral party with a checklist of the elements a crime requires. Three out of four is not enough. Prosecutors judged on their win rate, he said, will be loath to bring frivolous cases. {#winrate}
## The citizens’ veto

The second layer was invented in the UK around the 14th and 15th centuries, when people felt the state had too much discretion: a grand jury of citizens who must agree there is enough to indict. It largely faded there, because juries were too often overawed by prosecutors. {003-S05}

Citizens, Shah said, need to be imbued with public choice theory and scepticism. And the indictment of Donald Trump in the US raised a new problem: in a random sample of people, some 30 per cent are politically radicalised. {#radical}
~ Copying the US, the UK or Japan will not work, Shah said. Building the republic means many hard problems, each “a twenty year, forty year, sixty year journey”. {003-C09}

quote.text: Once you have a point of view, the entire universe organizes itself to give you facts that enhance and support your belief.

sections.label: The third idea
sections.head: The patient wants ivermectin
sections.caption: the dharma of a profession
body: Every calling has a dharma, Amit Varma said. A lawyer serves the client, but within the law. A doctor heals. A journalist speaks truth to power or, in the old maxim, afflicts the comfortable and comforts the afflicted. {003-J09}

Each is pulled the other way by an incentive to give people what they demand. A doctor’s dharma, Varma said, is to do what is best for the patient; the incentive is to give the patient what he wants, even the wrong thing. {003-C10}
A journalist working for a media organisation may likewise give the market one side of a narrative battle rather than the truth.
His friend Murali Neelakantan, for many years a law-firm partner in the UK and the US, came back to India and took on a client who expected him to lie on his behalf. {003-S07}
## Parents, then courts
Ajay Shah said dharma is shaped first by parents, then, as Varma suggested with UK courts and perjury, by institutions.
~ Echoing their friend Suyash Rai, Shah added that the state is neither necessary nor sufficient. Most of our moral code is enforced between people, and the state should do only a small part of it.

quote.text: In England perjury is the exception and it ends a lawyer’s career if you do it. But in India it is a norm.
quote.who: Murali Neelakantan, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: Free lessons in liberty
sections.caption: Eamonn Butler’s primers
body: People often ask Amit Varma what to read to understand individual freedom, classical liberalism, or thinkers he admires such as Adam Smith and Hayek. He thinks it a really important question.

Many ideas we pick up by osmosis when young, he said, make us feel incredibly virtuous, as if we were serving social justice. They tend to be ideas of socialism, which implicitly use the coercive power of the state: deeply illiberal ideas. {003-J10}
## A shelf of primers

His answer is a series by Eamonn Butler, who works at a think tank in the UK and is, in Varma’s opinion, one of the finest liberal minds in the world. Butler has primers on classical liberalism, Hayek, Mises, Milton Friedman, public choice and Adam Smith. {003-R01}

The public choice primer he called outstanding, because the books of Buchanan and Tullock can make for complex reading. So can Hayek’s, “though what a great writer”. Butler, Varma said, gets to the heart of each subject and breaks it down beautifully.
~ The primers are sold as cheap Kindle books and can also be had free on the website. “These books are an education,” Varma said, “and it is a miracle that they are free.”

quote.text: A lot of the ideas that we pick up by osmosis when we are young are ideas that make us feel incredibly virtuous

sections.label: Ajay’s anti-pick
sections.head: Dirty soil, better salad
sections.caption: the root microbiome
body: Ajay Shah came with no recommendation, only an anti-recommendation, for something nobody should do: hydroponics, the “little cult” of growing leaves and vegetables in water with nutrients.
Its appeal, he said, is superficial. Hydroponic vegetables are very clean: they do not come from the mess of the soil, they carry no insects or worms, and they need less washing.
## What lives below
The insight lies in the root microbiome. The human gut, Shah said, holds one to two kilograms of bacteria and yeasts that make complex chemicals the body uses. {#gut}

In the same way, a plant growing in soil relies on a root microbiome that constructs complex chemicals for it. Kill it with chemical fertilisers, pesticides or excessive ploughing, or grow the plant in water, and its nutrients are systematically inferior. {003-C12}

His advice is to favour the mess of soil that has not been ploughed and has not faced chemical fertilisers or pesticides. Amit Varma had a different objection to leaves. “Anybody who’s eating a leaf, it’s a superficial joy only,” he said. {003-J11}
~ Both hosts are excited by meat grown in a lab. Varma came to it by way of Tolstoy’s chicken on the chair. {003-S09}

quote.text: We should look beyond the superficial happiness that we get out of having a pristine leaf

side.boxText: Tourists now expect pink, but Jaipur’s pinkness is not ancient, Amit Varma read. He does not know why that colour was chosen. In 1876, he said, the city was painted pink to commemorate a visit by Prince Edward. {#pink}

contQuote.text: So all of us are creatures are made by social programming. We can’t deny it. We can’t will it away. We can’t wish it away. It is there. Our only choice is to become self-aware.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A live chicken, a sweet question, a doctor’s restraint and an economist’s confession

stories.start: a story I want to tell you about this, which is about Leo Tolstoy
stories.end: The chick chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.
stories.caption: Tolstoy’s live chicken
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Tolstoy, his aunt and a dinner invitation
stories.head: The meal that squawked back
body: In the last years of his life, Amit Varma said, Leo Tolstoy was “an incredibly self-righteous, virtue signaling old man” who lectured everyone: don’t do this, don’t do that, peace and love. One of the things he cared about most was not eating animals.

One day his aunt, older still, Varma guessed, announced that she was coming to dinner. She wanted chicken, and none of Tolstoy’s talk about vegetarians. Tolstoy agreed: come, he told her, and you will have chicken.
The aunt duly arrived and was taken to the dining table. On her chair sat a live chicken, going squawk, squawk, squawk. {#squawk}
“You wanted a chicken, there’s your chicken, have it,” Tolstoy told her, in Varma’s telling.

Varma wrote an essay on the story in the late nineties; it is no longer online anywhere. Under the influence of such noble thoughts, when he was some twenty years younger, he turned vegetarian for a year, out of compassion, but could not keep it up. {#veg}
To him the story names a gap we choose to ignore. “It’s a seen and the unseen,” he said. “The chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.” {003-S09}

~ Modern science may offer a way out, he said: meat grown in a lab, not a meat substitute, without the animal ever existing. One could grow a chicken leg or make a steak. We might have our meat and eat it too, “whatever that might mean”.
stories.why: Lab-grown meat, both hosts hope, might one day close a gap that Tolstoy forced into view: we enjoy the chicken on the plate because we never see the chicken on the chair. {003-C13}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah, too, is excited by lab-grown meat: it would be so nice, he said, to eat meat without harming any sentient creature.

stories.caption: the question at the book launch
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the listener who knew only his show self
stories.head: The man who never shouts?
body: At a book launch a while back, Amit Varma was approached by a couple who had heard every episode of his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen*. Both were regular listeners.
The wife asked him, sweetly and sincerely, a question: had he ever shouted at someone in his life? {003-S02}
Varma felt terrible. She knew him only from the show, and had taken its persona for the whole man. That persona, he said, may be authentic to him, “but it’s not all that I am”.

~ The danger is that an audience mistakes a slice for the whole, and in time the person may too. People contain multitudes, Varma argued, and a persona that wins approval can shut out the rest. {003-C01}

quote.text: This person simply just know me from the show and that’s my persona.

stories.end: at a particular point in time to goggle with. But that was it.
stories.caption: overtreatment during COVID
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what a doctor told him about overtreatment
stories.head: Paracetamol, and nothing else
body: The doctor Lancelot Pinto told Amit Varma that during COVID a significant percentage of the deaths were caused by overtreatment. {003-S08}

Patients would go to a doctor and insist on what the neighbour had got, ivermectin and all. Overtreatment could set off a cytokine storm, and its results, Varma said if he remembered correctly, really started after about a week.
When Varma himself got COVID, Pinto gave him paracetamol and something to gargle with. “And that’s it, nothing else,” Varma said.
~ For Varma, it shows the gap between a doctor’s dharma, to do what is best for the patient, and the incentive to give patients what they want, even when they want the wrong thing. {003-C10}
stories.why: A profession’s duty and its incentives can pull opposite ways. When patients demand more medicine, the doctor who gives less may be the one keeping to his calling, as Pinto did with Varma.

stories.start: The first is that I was part of The economic policy process
stories.end: if the knowledge is there, then it can. reach out and have an impact
stories.caption: the laws he helped amend
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why the reforms he worked on fell short
stories.head: Economists who knew too little
body: Amit Varma asked why any government would give up the tools it uses to harass its enemies. Ajay Shah answered with a confession.

He had been part of the economic policy process and helped amend laws in an age when the opportunity to do things right was “sky high”. They were not done well, he said, “because of intellectual failures of people like me”. {003-S06}
Mainline economists like him saw the world through the lens of economics. They lacked knowledge of law, public administration and checks and balances, and assumed civil servants were basically good.

~ Only in the last 10 to 20 years, he said, has India come to grips with these problems in a deeper way. {#decades} He stays optimistic: moments for reform keep coming, and when the knowledge is there, it can have an impact.
stories.why: Missed reforms are not always about bad intentions. Sometimes the knowledge is missing when the window opens, so building it in advance is how to be ready for the next one.

quiz.q: According to Amit Varma, why was Jaipur painted pink in the first place?
quiz.a: To commemorate a visit by Prince Edward in 1876, though he doesn’t know why pink.

quiz.q: Why did Fox News carry the stolen-election theories, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Its audience ran away when it told the truth; it was a business decision.

quiz.q: What did a grand jury decide, and why did it fade in the UK?
quiz.a: Whether to indict; juries were too often overawed by prosecutors and simply agreed.

quiz.q: What did Lancelot Pinto give Amit Varma when Varma got COVID?
quiz.a: Paracetamol and something to gargle with, and nothing else at all.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah say hydroponic growing removes from a plant, and why does it matter?
quiz.a: The root microbiome, which makes complex chemicals; without it, nutrition is systematically inferior.

quiz.q: What greeted Tolstoy’s aunt when she came to dinner demanding chicken?
quiz.a: A live chicken on her chair, squawking: there’s your chicken, have it.
